questions.q: Which event that began in 1789 is regarded as a major starting point of modern nationalism in Europe?
questions.explanation: The French Revolution of 1789 spread the idea that sovereignty belongs to the people, who together form the nation.

questions.q: In which year was the Civil Code, popularly called the Napoleonic Code, introduced in France?
questions.explanation: Napoleon introduced the Civil Code in 1804.

questions.q: Which of the following was a feature of the Napoleonic Code of 1804?
options: Restoration of privileges based on birth
Equality before the law and the right to property
Revival of feudal dues for peasants
questions.explanation: The Code did away with birth-based privileges, established equality before the law and secured the right to property.

questions.q: Who was the Austrian chancellor who hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815?
questions.explanation: Duke Metternich of Austria hosted the Congress, which aimed to undo much of what Napoleon had changed.

questions.q: The conservative governments set up after 1815 imposed strict censorship mainly because they
options: feared that newspapers and books would spread liberal and nationalist ideas
wanted to protect the profits of printers
had been ordered to do so by Napoleon
wished to protect the copyright of authors
questions.explanation: Conservative rulers saw liberal and nationalist ideas as threats to monarchy and the old social order, so they tried to control what was published.

questions.q: Why was the Prussian-led customs union (Zollverein) of 1834 important for German unification?
options: It created a single German army
It removed tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies, linking German states economically
It gave the Prussian king the title of emperor
It set up the Frankfurt Parliament
questions.explanation: By abolishing tariff barriers and cutting the number of currencies, the Zollverein tied the German states together economically and strengthened a sense of nationhood.

questions.q: Who was Giuseppe Mazzini, and what was his contribution to nationalism in Italy and Europe?
questions.answer: Mazzini was an Italian revolutionary who believed Italy should become a single unified republic. He founded the secret societies Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne, which inspired similar movements elsewhere.
keyPoints: Italian revolutionary who wanted a unified republic
Founded Young Italy
Founded Young Europe, with members from several countries
questions.explanation: Mazzini’s societies spread the ideal of nation-states based on the will of the people.

questions.q: Explain how Otto von Bismarck used war to build the German nation-state.
questions.answer: Bismarck, the Prussian chief minister, used the Prussian army and bureaucracy. In a series of wars against Denmark, Austria and France, Prussia won, and in January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles.
keyPoints: Prussia led unification under Bismarck
Wars with Denmark, Austria and France ended in victory
William I proclaimed emperor in 1871
questions.explanation: Unification was achieved by Prussian military power and diplomacy rather than by a popular liberal movement.

questions.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 gave the government the power to
options: ban the import of foreign cloth
questions.explanation: The Act allowed detention of political prisoners for two years without trial, which Indians saw as unjust.

questions.q: In which city did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of April 1919 take place?
questions.explanation: On 13 April 1919 General Dyer’s troops fired on a crowd gathered in Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar.

questions.q: From which ashram did Gandhiji begin the Salt March in 1930?
questions.explanation: The march began at Sabarmati Ashram near Ahmedabad and ended at Dandi on the Gujarat coast.

questions.q: The Khilafat Movement was launched mainly to
options: demand an end to the salt tax
protest against the harsh treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War
questions.explanation: Muslim leaders such as the Ali brothers protested against the treatment of the Caliph, and Gandhiji linked this cause with the Non-Cooperation Movement.

questions.q: Why did Gandhiji call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?
options: The British had accepted all the demands
The Congress had lost the elections
The violence at Chauri Chaura convinced him that the movement was turning violent
He had been arrested by the government
questions.explanation: After a mob set a police station on fire at Chauri Chaura, Gandhiji, committed to non-violence, withdrew the movement.

questions.q: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted in India?
options: It proposed to abolish the Congress
It demanded higher taxes from peasants
It was headed by an Indian industrialist
It had no Indian member although it was to decide India’s constitutional future
questions.explanation: All members were British, so Indians felt excluded; protesters shouted ‘Simon go back’.

questions.q: What was the Poona Pact of 1932?
questions.answer: It was an agreement between Gandhiji and Dr B. R. Ambedkar. After Gandhiji’s fast against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, the pact gave them reserved seats in the legislative councils, to be voted for by the general electorate.
keyPoints: Agreement between Gandhiji and Ambedkar in 1932
Followed Gandhiji’s fast against separate electorates
Reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in the legislatures
questions.explanation: The pact settled the dispute over separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

questions.q: Why did Gandhiji choose salt as the issue on which to challenge British rule in 1930?
questions.answer: Salt was used by every household, rich or poor, and the tax on it hurt the poor most. It could unite people of all classes. Gandhiji marched to Dandi and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930, beginning the Civil Disobedience Movement.
keyPoints: Everyone used salt, so it united all classes
The salt tax and monopoly burdened the poor
Breaking the salt law at Dandi launched Civil Disobedience
questions.explanation: Salt was a simple and powerful symbol of unjust colonial rule.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The ancient Silk Routes linked Asia with
questions.explanation: The Silk Routes were trade and cultural links connecting Asia, Europe and northern Africa.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which American industrialist is known for introducing assembly-line production of cars?
questions.explanation: Henry Ford’s assembly line made cars cheaper and encouraged mass production and mass consumption.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Corn Laws, which Britain abolished in 1846, had restricted the
questions.explanation: The Corn Laws limited grain imports; when they were abolished, cheaper food flowed into Britain.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Indentured labourers were
options: skilled artisans hired by factories at fixed wages
workers bound by a contract to work for an employer for a fixed number of years
questions.explanation: Indentured labourers signed contracts and were taken to plantations in distant colonies; many were from poor regions of India.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Great Depression that began around 1929 hit farmers especially hard mainly because
options: agricultural prices fell sharply as production exceeded demand
farmers refused to sell their grain
questions.explanation: Overproduction of crops pushed prices down, and farmers’ incomes collapsed.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: The Bretton Woods conference of 1944 led to the setting up of
options: the League of Nations and the WHO
the IMF and the World Bank
questions.explanation: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank were created to manage the post-war international economy.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: How did foods from the Americas, such as the potato, change life in Europe?
questions.answer: The potato was cheap and grew well in poor soil, so it became a staple food of poorer Europeans. Their diet and health improved and the population grew, although dependence on one crop caused the Irish potato famine when it was struck by disease.
keyPoints: Potato became a staple of the poor
Better nutrition and population growth
Over-dependence led to famine in Ireland in the 1840s
questions.explanation: New foods from the Americas changed diets, but depending on one crop was risky.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Why is the Great Depression described as a global event?
questions.answer: It began in the USA after the stock market crash of 1929, but American banks recalled loans from Europe and trade collapsed. Prices, production and employment fell in many countries, including colonies such as India whose exports fell sharply.
keyPoints: Started in the USA around 1929
Loans were recalled and world trade fell
Affected many countries including colonies
questions.explanation: Because economies were linked through trade and finance, the crisis spread worldwide.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which country was the first to industrialise?
questions.explanation: Industrialisation began in Britain in the 18th century, first with cotton textiles.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which inventor improved the steam engine in the late 18th century, making it widely useful in industry?
questions.explanation: James Watt improved Newcomen’s steam engine, which powered factories and later transport.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Proto-industrialisation refers to
options: production in the countryside by peasant households for merchants, before the rise of factories
the use of electricity in factories
the setting up of trade unions
questions.explanation: Merchants in towns gave raw material to rural families who spun and wove at home; this preceded factory production.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: In which year was the first cotton mill in Bombay set up?
questions.explanation: Bombay’s first cotton mill came up in 1854.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did many employers in Victorian Britain still prefer hand labour to machines in some industries?
options: Hand labour was always costlier than machines
Where demand was seasonal or varied, hand labour was cheaper and more flexible
questions.explanation: Machines were costly and suited to standard goods, while labour was plentiful and could be hired when needed.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: In Indian mills, jobbers were usually
options: owners of cotton fields supplying raw material
trusted workers who recruited new labourers and helped them settle, often demanding money and favours
questions.explanation: Jobbers were intermediaries between mill owners and workers and gained power over those they recruited.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: What was the role of the gomasthas appointed by the East India Company in Bengal?
questions.answer: Gomasthas were paid servants of the Company who supervised weavers, collected the cloth and checked its quality. They replaced the traders and brokers who had earlier dealt with weavers, which reduced the weavers’ bargaining power.
keyPoints: Paid servants of the Company
Supervised weavers, collected cloth, examined quality
Reduced weavers’ freedom to bargain
questions.explanation: The Company used gomasthas to control supply and cut out middlemen.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Why did cheap machine-made cloth from Britain hurt Indian weavers in the 19th century?
questions.answer: Cheap Manchester cloth flooded Indian markets and undersold handloom cloth. At the same time raw cotton was exported to Britain, making it costly for Indian weavers. Weaving centres such as Surat and Hooghly declined.
keyPoints: Imports of cheap factory cloth undersold handloom cloth
Raw cotton became costly because of exports
Old weaving centres declined
questions.explanation: Competition from imports and scarcity of raw cotton squeezed Indian weavers.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: In which country did printing technology first develop?
questions.explanation: Hand printing with woodblocks began in China and later spread to Japan and Europe.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Who developed the printing press with movable metal type in Germany in the 1430s?
questions.explanation: Gutenberg built the first printing press with movable type; the Bible was among his first major books.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Martin Luther’s Ninety-Five Theses of 1517 criticised
options: practices and teachings of the Roman Catholic Church
questions.explanation: Luther’s writings, widely printed, began the Protestant Reformation.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Which of these men edited the Bengal Gazette, one of the earliest newspapers in India?
questions.explanation: James Augustus Hickey started the weekly Bengal Gazette in 1780.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: How did print help ideas of thinkers such as Voltaire and Rousseau reach more people before the French Revolution?
options: Their books and pamphlets were printed in large numbers and discussed beyond the elite
Their ideas were taught in every school
Kings had ordered their works to be read aloud
Their writings were kept secret in libraries
questions.explanation: Print made ideas about reason, rights and liberty widely available, encouraging public debate.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Why did the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 provoke criticism in India?
options: It promoted Indian languages in schools
It gave the government wide powers to censor reports and editorials in Indian-language newspapers
questions.explanation: The Act aimed to control the nationalist press, which is why it was widely criticised.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: What was Johann Gutenberg’s contribution to printing?
questions.answer: Gutenberg developed the printing press in Germany around the 1430s, adapting the olive and wine press and using metal moulds to cast letters. He printed the Bible, making books faster and cheaper to produce.
keyPoints: Developed the printing press in Germany
Used movable metal type
Printed the Bible
questions.explanation: His press allowed books to be produced in large numbers.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Why did the Roman Catholic Church try to control printed books after the spread of print?
questions.answer: Print spread new and critical interpretations of the faith that challenged the Church’s authority. The Church imposed controls on publishers and booksellers and from 1558 maintained an Index of Prohibited Books.
keyPoints: Print spread ideas that questioned Church authority
Controls on printers and booksellers
Index of Prohibited Books from 1558
questions.explanation: Rulers and the Church feared that print could spread dissenting ideas.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic resource?
questions.explanation: Abiotic resources are non-living, such as rocks and metals.

questions.q: The Rio de Janeiro Earth Summit of 1992 endorsed
questions.explanation: Agenda 21 was adopted at Rio in 1992 as a plan for sustainable development in the 21st century.

questions.q: Which soil is formed by deposits of the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers and is very fertile?
questions.explanation: Alluvial soil is carried and laid down by rivers and covers the northern plains.

questions.q: Black soil is particularly well suited to growing
questions.explanation: Black soil holds moisture well and is ideal for cotton, so it is also called black cotton soil.

questions.q: Laterite soil is poor in nutrients mainly because
options: it is made only of sand
heavy rain washes away (leaches) soluble nutrients, leaving mostly iron and aluminium compounds
questions.explanation: Under heavy rain the soil is leached, which is why laterite needs manure and fertiliser.

questions.q: Ploughing across the slope along contour lines helps because it
options: increases the speed of water flow
stops rain entering the soil completely
slows run-off water and reduces soil erosion
questions.explanation: Contour ploughing slows water running down a slope, so less soil is washed away.

questions.q: Classify resources on the basis of ownership and give one example of each type.
questions.answer: Individual resources, such as a house or plot of land; community resources, such as village commons or parks; national resources, which include all resources within the nation’s territory; and international resources, such as the open ocean beyond the Exclusive Economic Zone.
keyPoints: Individual: house or plot
Community: commons, parks
National: all resources within a nation
International: open ocean beyond the EEZ
questions.explanation: Ownership decides who may use and manage a resource.

questions.q: What is sustainable development, and why is it needed?
questions.answer: Sustainable development means developing without harming the environment and without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs. It is needed because overuse of resources leads to depletion and environmental damage.
keyPoints: Development without damaging the environment
Keeps resources available for future generations
Needed because of overuse and depletion
questions.explanation: It balances present economic needs with long-term protection of resources.

questions.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
questions.explanation: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in summer, so it is a rabi crop.

questions.q: Jhumming is a type of
questions.explanation: In jhumming, farmers clear land by cutting and burning vegetation, mostly in north-eastern India.

questions.q: Which of these is a plantation crop?
questions.explanation: Tea is grown on large estates, usually as a single crop, which is the mark of plantation agriculture.

questions.q: The Bhoodan movement started by Vinoba Bhave aimed to
options: persuade landowners to donate land to the landless
questions.explanation: Vinoba Bhave walked from village to village asking landowners to give part of their land to the landless.

questions.q: Why are pulses often grown in rotation with other crops?
options: They are legumes that restore nitrogen to the soil
They need no water at all
They can be harvested within a week
questions.explanation: Leguminous plants fix nitrogen in the soil, helping the next crop.

questions.q: Which problem is commonly associated with large multipurpose dams?
options: Displacement of local communities and loss of land and forest
They always increase soil erosion everywhere
questions.explanation: Large dams submerge land and villages, so people lose homes and livelihoods; this led to movements such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan.

questions.q: What is rainwater harvesting? Name two traditional methods used in India.
questions.answer: Rainwater harvesting is collecting and storing rain for later use. Traditional methods include tankas in Rajasthan, khadins and johads, kuls in the hills, and bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
keyPoints: Collecting and storing rainwater
Any two methods such as tankas, johads, kuls, khadins
questions.explanation: Harvesting rain recharges groundwater and reduces dependence on distant sources.

questions.q: Why was the Green Revolution of the 1960s introduced in India, and what were its effects?
questions.answer: India faced food shortages. High-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation were introduced, which raised wheat and rice production, mainly in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. It also widened regional differences and caused heavy use of chemicals and groundwater.
keyPoints: Food shortages in the 1960s
High-yielding seeds, fertilisers, irrigation
Higher production but regional differences and environmental costs
questions.explanation: It improved food supply but had side-effects.

questions.q: Which of the following is a ferrous mineral?
questions.explanation: Ferrous minerals contain iron; iron ore is the main one.

questions.q: Which type of iron ore has the highest iron content, up to about 70 per cent?
questions.explanation: Magnetite is the finest iron ore with the highest iron content.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-conventional source of energy?
questions.explanation: Wind, solar, tidal and geothermal power are non-conventional, renewable sources.

questions.q: Jharia and Raniganj are well known for
questions.explanation: Jharia in Jharkhand and Raniganj in West Bengal are important coalfields in the Damodar valley region.

questions.q: Why are iron and steel plants usually located near sources of raw material such as iron ore and coal?
options: Steel is not sold in cities
The raw materials are heavy and costly to transport, so nearby location lowers costs
Rivers cannot be used near towns
questions.explanation: Bulky raw materials make transport costly; locating nearby cuts production costs.

questions.q: Which step helps reduce water pollution caused by factories?
options: Dumping hot water directly into rivers
Treating effluents before releasing them into rivers
questions.explanation: Treating waste water removes harmful substances before it enters rivers.

questions.q: Distinguish between conventional and non-conventional sources of energy, with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Conventional sources, such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and hydroelectricity, have long been in common use and many are exhaustible. Non-conventional sources, such as solar, wind, tidal and geothermal energy, are renewable and cleaner.
keyPoints: Conventional: coal, petroleum, natural gas, hydel
Non-conventional: solar, wind, tidal, geothermal
Non-conventional sources are renewable and cleaner
questions.explanation: The key difference is how widely they are used and whether they are renewable.

questions.q: Why is the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 often cited in discussions of industrial safety?
questions.answer: A leak of poisonous methyl isocyanate gas from a pesticide plant in Bhopal in December 1984 killed thousands and harmed the health of many more for years. It showed the need for strict safety rules and responsibility in industry.
keyPoints: Gas leak from a pesticide plant in Bhopal, 1984
Thousands died and many suffered lasting harm
Shows the need for safety regulation
questions.explanation: It is one of the worst industrial disasters and led to stricter environmental rules.

questions.q: In Belgium as a whole, which language group forms the majority?
questions.explanation: A majority of Belgians live in the Dutch-speaking region, while a large minority speak French.

questions.q: Which language was made the sole official language of Sri Lanka by an Act of 1956?
questions.explanation: The 1956 Act recognised only Sinhala as the official language, ignoring Tamil.

questions.q: Subjects such as defence and currency are included in the
questions.explanation: The Union List has subjects of national importance on which only the Union Parliament can make laws.

questions.q: Education and forests are included in the
questions.explanation: Both the Union and the states can make laws on Concurrent List subjects.

questions.q: Why is power sharing considered desirable in a democracy?
options: It reduces the possibility of conflict among social groups and respects the people’s voice
It ensures that one group rules forever
It removes the need for elections
questions.explanation: Sharing power makes government more acceptable to different groups and reduces tension.

questions.q: India is called a ‘holding together’ federation because
options: independent states joined by choice to form a bigger unit
a large country divided power between the Centre and the states to keep the nation united
the states have more power than the Union
questions.explanation: In holding-together federations, a large country shares power between the national and state governments.

questions.q: What is the Gram Sabha and what is its role in local government?
questions.answer: The Gram Sabha consists of all adult voters of a village. It meets to discuss and approve the work of the gram panchayat and holds it accountable.
keyPoints: All adult voters of a village
Discusses and approves panchayat work
Keeps the panchayat accountable
questions.explanation: The Gram Sabha is the base of village-level democracy.

questions.q: How did the Belgian arrangement reduce tension between its language communities?
questions.answer: The constitution was amended so that the central government has an equal number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers. State governments are not subordinate to the central government, Brussels has a separate government with equal representation, and a community government handles cultural and language matters.
keyPoints: Equal Dutch and French ministers in the central government
Separate government for Brussels with equal representation
Community government for cultural and language matters
questions.explanation: Sharing power among communities prevented conflict from splitting the country.

questions.q: What is the minimum voting age for Indian citizens?
questions.explanation: The voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 years by a constitutional amendment in 1988.

questions.q: In a democracy, the rulers are
questions.explanation: Democracy is a form of government in which rulers are elected by the people.

questions.q: Which of these is a function of political parties?
questions.explanation: Parties put up candidates, form governments if they win, or serve as opposition.

questions.q: When no single party wins a majority in a multi-party system, what often follows?
questions.explanation: Parties join together to form a coalition with enough members for a majority.

questions.q: Why are free and fair elections essential for democracy?
options: They guarantee that a particular party wins
They remove the need for an opposition
They let citizens choose and remove their rulers peacefully
questions.explanation: Regular, fair elections give people real control over those who govern them.

questions.q: Why was an anti-defection law considered necessary?
options: To force members to vote at random
To increase the number of parties
To stop elected legislators from changing parties for personal gain
questions.explanation: Frequent defections made governments unstable, so a law was passed to discourage members from switching parties.

questions.q: State any three functions of political parties in a democracy.
questions.answer: Parties contest elections, put forward policies and programmes, make laws through their legislators, form and run governments, act as opposition, shape public opinion and help people reach government schemes.
keyPoints: Contest elections
Form governments or act as opposition
Make policies and laws
Shape public opinion
questions.explanation: Parties connect citizens with government.

questions.q: Explain two challenges faced by political parties in India and one way to reduce them.
questions.answer: Many parties lack internal democracy, with power concentrated in a few leaders or families. Money and muscle power also influence elections. Requiring parties to hold regular organisational elections and candidates to disclose their assets and cases can help.
keyPoints: Lack of internal democracy or dynastic succession
Money and muscle power
A reform such as disclosure by candidates or regular party elections
questions.explanation: Parties must be accountable and transparent to keep faith in democracy.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Dairy farming belongs to which sector of the economy?
questions.explanation: Dairy produces a natural product directly, so it is part of the primary sector.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: GDP stands for
questions.explanation: GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Per capita income is calculated by
options: adding up the profits of all firms
dividing total income by the total population
dividing total income by the number of earners
questions.explanation: Per capita income is the average income per person.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act of 2005 guarantees
options: a government job to every graduate
100 days of employment in a year to a rural household willing to do manual work
questions.explanation: The Act aims to give rural households work for 100 days a year.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why does disguised unemployment occur in agriculture?
options: More people are engaged in work than needed, so removing some would not reduce output
There is no land to farm
Farm work is done only by machines
questions.explanation: On a small plot, extra family members appear to be working, but output would be the same without them.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why is per capita income alone not a sufficient measure of development?
options: It does not show how income is distributed or what people’s health and education are like
It always falls when a country grows
Only large countries have per capita income
questions.explanation: An average can hide inequality and says little about health, education and quality of life.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Distinguish between the organised and unorganised sectors.
questions.answer: The organised sector consists of registered enterprises with regular working hours, job security and benefits. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units, irregular and low-paid work, and little protection or job security.
keyPoints: Organised: registered, regular hours, security and benefits
Unorganised: small scattered units, irregular low pay
Little protection in the unorganised sector
questions.explanation: The difference lies in regulation and the security workers enjoy.

questions.topic: Development and the Sectors of the Economy
questions.q: Why are only final goods and services counted in GDP?
questions.answer: Intermediate goods are used up in producing final goods and their value is already included in the final price. Counting them as well would count the same value twice, which is called double counting.
keyPoints: Intermediate goods are included in the value of final goods
Counting them would cause double counting
questions.explanation: Counting only final goods gives a correct total.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: A situation in which each party has what the other wants is called
questions.explanation: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants, which is why money was a great improvement.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Which institution is the central bank of India?
questions.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India supervises banks and issues currency.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Collateral is
options: an asset pledged by a borrower as a guarantee until the loan is repaid
the interest paid on a deposit
questions.explanation: If the borrower fails to repay, the lender can sell the collateral to recover the loan.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Globalisation means
options: isolating a country’s economy from others
rapid integration between countries through trade and investment
questions.explanation: Globalisation links countries through the movement of goods, services, investment and technology.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why do many multinational companies set up production in countries with low labour costs?
options: Because prices are fixed by law everywhere
It lowers their cost of production and raises profit while they sell in the world market
They are required to by international law
questions.explanation: Lower wages and costs help MNCs earn higher profits.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: Why were three-tier consumer courts set up under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986?
options: To give consumers a simple, quick and low-cost way to seek redress
questions.explanation: District, State and National commissions help consumers settle complaints without costly court cases.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: What are the main terms of credit that a borrower must agree to?
questions.answer: The terms of credit are the interest rate, the collateral required, the documentation needed and the mode of repayment.
keyPoints: Interest rate
Collateral
Documentation
Mode of repayment
questions.explanation: These terms differ between lenders and affect how costly a loan is.

questions.topic: Money, Credit, Globalisation and Consumer Rights
questions.q: How do Self Help Groups help poor women reduce dependence on moneylenders?
questions.answer: Members, usually 15 to 20 women, pool small savings and give loans from the common fund at reasonable interest. This gives them credit without collateral from moneylenders and builds the habit of saving.
keyPoints: Members save small amounts regularly
Loans given from the group fund at reasonable interest
Reduces dependence on moneylenders
questions.explanation: Group savings give poor households a source of cheap credit.

questions.q: Who was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871?
questions.explanation: William I of Prussia was proclaimed Emperor of the new German Empire in 1871.

questions.q: The Indian National Congress was founded in
questions.explanation: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.

questions.topic: The Making of a Global World
questions.q: Which food crop was introduced to Europe from the Americas?
questions.explanation: The potato, along with maize and tomato, came from the Americas.

questions.topic: Industrialisation and the Age of Industry
questions.q: Which industry was at the centre of Britain’s early industrialisation?
questions.explanation: Cotton textile mills in places such as Lancashire led early industrialisation.

questions.topic: Print Culture and the Modern World
questions.q: Chapbooks in Europe were
options: small cheap books sold by pedlars called chapmen
questions.explanation: Chapbooks were pocket-sized and affordable, sold by travelling pedlars.

questions.q: Which soil is also known as regur soil?
questions.explanation: Black soil is also called regur soil.

questions.q: Distinguish between rabi and kharif crops with two examples of each.
questions.answer: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in summer, for example wheat and mustard. Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon and harvested in September–October, for example rice and cotton.
keyPoints: Rabi: sown in winter, harvested in summer, e.g. wheat
Kharif: sown with monsoon, harvested in autumn, e.g. rice
questions.explanation: The cropping seasons depend on sowing and harvesting times.

questions.q: Why is the conservation of minerals necessary?
questions.answer: Minerals are formed over millions of years and are non-renewable, so they can run out. Conserving them through recycling, efficient use and substitutes keeps supplies available for the future.
keyPoints: Minerals are non-renewable
Take millions of years to form
Recycling and efficient use help conserve them
questions.explanation: Limited mineral stocks must be used carefully.
